Hi, doctor. Yeah, um, I’m a barber. I’m 27, I’ve been cutting hair since I graduated, and I usually really love the work, the atmosphere in the shop, talking to the guys... but I’m here because it’s just gotten to the point where my job is practically on the line, and my nerves are completely shot. 

It’s the straight razors. I mean, it sounds ridiculous, right? A barber having an issue with a razor. But I’ve gotten to where I will do almost absolutely anything to avoid using the straight razor at work. I’ll look at the appointment book, and if someone is scheduled for a hot lather shave or a tight neck cleanup, I’ll beg one of the other barbers to switch clients with me. I'll make up any excuse I can think of. If I can't get someone to swap, I'll just lie to the client. I’ll say the blade’s missing, or I'm out of replacements. Sometimes I actually take the razor and bury it all the way in the back of my station drawer under my clippers and combs so I can pretend I can't find it. It takes up so much of my mental energy just plotting how to get out of using it every single day. 

And... and the worst part is, if I can’t get out of it, like if the owner is standing right there watching me and I have absolutely no choice but to do it, it's an absolute nightmare. I’m literally shaking through the whole shave. My hand is just trembling the entire time I'm holding this incredibly sharp blade near someone's skin, and I'm just sweating and tense, just praying I don't slip. It feels like the shave takes hours. You know, it’s funny you ask that, because people—well, the few people who actually know about this—they always assume I must be terrified of knives in general. But honestly? No. Not at all. I mean, at home, I actually do a lot of the cooking. I have this really nice set of Japanese chef knives that I bought a couple of years ago, and they are incredibly sharp. Like, cut-through-a-tomato-like-butter sharp. And I can stand there and chop vegetables, slice up a roast, whatever, and I don’t even think twice about it. My heart rate doesn't go up, my hands are perfectly steady... it’s totally fine. 

Same with scissors. Like, normal hair-cutting shears? Totally fine. I can do a scissor cut all day long, snipping right next to someone's ear, and I don't feel a thing. Box cutters when I’m opening packages, steak knives at a restaurant, shaving my own face with a regular Gillette cartridge razor... no sweat at all. It really is just... it’s just that specific type of blade, the straight razor. 

I don’t even own one at home anymore, actually. I used to have one in my bathroom for my own neck, back when I was in barber school and practicing, but once this whole thing started getting bad, I just threw it out. I actually wrapped it up in like three layers of paper towels and took it straight out to the apartment dumpster because I just didn't even want to risk seeing it in the drawer when I was looking for my toothpaste. But yeah, if I’m just making dinner or using a normal knife, I’m completely fine. It’s weird, right? Like, a sharp edge is a sharp edge, you’d think my brain would react the exact same way, but it just doesn't. It's only that specific folding handle and that long, exposed edge of the straight razor... but normal sharp stuff at home? Nothing. I'm totally relaxed.

I’ve sat up at night, just staring at the ceiling, trying to figure out if there was some... some specific moment, you know? Like, did I slip? Did I see someone else slip? But no. Nothing. Never.

I even tried to think if maybe I saw a movie when I was a kid, like Sweeney Todd or something, that just buried itself in my subconscious, but I didn't even watch movies like that! My parents were super strict about what we watched on TV. So there is just no logical reason for it. It just started creeping up on me out of nowhere. One week I was totally fine doing a hot lather shave, and the next week my palms were getting a little sweaty, and then a month later I'm practically hyperventilating in the breakroom trying to get out of a basic neck trim. So no, no accidents, no close calls, no nothing. It’s completely irrational, and I just don't know why it's happening.

Oh man, yeah. It’s not just when it’s actually in my hand. It’s... it’s like a hair-trigger reaction now.

I have to turn my whole body away. Even just seeing the blade exposed, just catching the light from the shop windows, it sends this shock straight through me. My stomach drops. 

I actually arrange my whole station so my own razors are completely hidden, like I was saying before, just so I don't accidentally glance at them while I'm reaching for my clippers or my shears. Actually, no. And I know that probably sounds a little contradictory, considering how much of a wreck I am when I'm actually there, but... no, I really don't. When I'm at home, it's like my brain just completely compartmentalizes the whole thing.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
You know, surprisingly... no. Not at all. It is actually kind of funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day. I was watching Peaky Blinders on TV—I don't know if you have seen it, it is set in England back in the twenties, really gritty, great cinematography, Cillian Murphy is just incredible in it—and the main characters literally have straight razor blades sewn right into the brims of their caps. They take their hats off and use them as weapons in these massive, chaotic street fights. And I was just sitting there on my couch, totally relaxed, not even blinking. My heart rate didn't go up, my hands were completely dry. I was just watching it like any normal person would watch a TV show. 

And it is the exact same thing with pictures or social media. Being a barber, my entire Instagram and TikTok feed is basically just hair tutorials and barbershop videos. It is just how the algorithm works, you know? You watch one fade tutorial and suddenly your whole explore page is guys doing these super detailed, macro-lens videos of hot towel shaves, where you see the straight razor gliding right over the skin in slow motion. And I can watch those all day long! I actually really appreciate them. I will look at the video and think, oh man, his blade angle is perfect, or I will wonder if he is using a Feather Artist Club razor or maybe a Parker handle. My brain just goes into total analytical barber mode. There is absolutely zero panic. 

Even if someone is just talking about it, like if I am out grabbing a coffee and a buddy mentions getting a really good straight razor shave at a shop downtown, I don't get that tight feeling in my chest at all. I can talk about the technique, the type of lather they used, the history of the tools, all of it, and I am completely fine. 

So it is definitely not the concept of the razor, if that makes sense. It is like my brain is smart enough to know that a picture on a screen or a video on my phone cannot physically reach out and hurt anybody. It is trapped behind the glass, so it is safe. It is only when the physical object is actually in the room with me, when it is real and tangible and the blade is actually exposed right in front of my face... that is when all the alarms start going off. But TV, movies, pictures, just talking about it... totally fine. It doesn't bother me in the slightest.

I actually wrapped it up in like three layers of paper towels and took it straight out to the apartment dumpster because I just didn't even want to risk seeing it in the drawer when I was looking for my toothpaste. But yeah, if I’m just making dinner or using a normal knife, I’m completely fine. It’s weird, right? Like, a sharp edge is a sharp edge, you’d think my brain would react the exact same way, but it just doesn't. It's only that specific folding handle and that long, exposed edge of the straight razor... but normal sharp stuff at home? Nothing. I'm totally relaxed.\n\nDoctor: Has there ever been a specific incident or event in the past where something went wrong or scared you while using a straight razor, like a slip, injury, or close call?\n\nPatient: No, and honestly, that’s the part that drives me absolutely crazy about all of this. I’ve wracked my brain, I really have. I’ve sat up at night, just staring at the ceiling, trying to figure out if there was some... some specific moment, you know? Like, did I slip? Did I see someone else slip? But no. Nothing. Never. \n\nI mean, when I was in barber school—this was back in like, 2018 or so—we spent weeks, literally weeks, just practicing on balloons. You know how they teach you? They put hot lather on an inflated balloon and you have to shave it clean without popping it. It teaches you pressure and blade angles. And doctor, I was the best in my class at it. I never popped a single balloon. Not one! \n\nAnd once I got on the floor with real clients? I’ve never given anyone a bad cut. I mean, sure, maybe a tiny, microscopic nick that you just dab with a styptic pencil and it stops in two seconds—literally every single barber in the world does that, it’s just part of the job. But a real injury? A slip? A close call where I almost hurt somebody or hit a vein? Never. I've never dropped an open razor, I've never had a client jump in the chair while I was working on their neck... nothing. My technique is actually really, really good. I'm meticulous about it. I always stretch the skin perfectly taut, I check my lighting... I'm incredibly safe. \n\nSo it makes absolutely zero sense. If I had slipped and given some guy a huge gash, I could totally understand why my brain is doing this. I could say, 'Okay, you're freaking out because of that awful thing that happened.' But I don't have that excuse! I even tried to think if maybe I saw a movie when I was a kid, like Sweeney Todd or something, that just buried itself in my subconscious, but I didn't even watch movies like that! My parents were super strict about what we watched on TV. So there is just no logical reason for it. It just started creeping up on me out of nowhere. One week I was totally fine doing a hot lather shave, and the next week my palms were getting a little sweaty, and then a month later I'm practically hyperventilating in the breakroom trying to get out of a basic neck trim. So no, no accidents, no close calls, no nothing. It’s completely irrational, and I just don't know why it's happening.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting anxious or avoiding things even when you're not holding the straight razor—like if someone else is using one nearby, or if you just see one on a shelf or even think about it?\n\nPatient: Oh man, yeah. It’s not just when it’s actually in my hand. It’s... it’s like a hair-trigger reaction now. \n\nI could just be sweeping up hair around my chair, totally fine, having a great day, chatting with a regular, and then I’ll hear the guy in my chair, or even the guy in the next chair over, say something like, \"Hey, can I get a hot towel and a razor shave on the neck?\" And doctor, the second—and I mean the literal second—I hear a client ask for the razor shave, it just hits me like a freight train. My chest immediately tightens up, almost like someone just yanked a belt tight around my ribs. My hands start getting incredibly sweaty, which is obviously awful when you're a barber, you know? You can't be working on someone's hair with damp hands. And it’s like my entire body just wants to physically back away before I even have time to think about it. It's this pure, raw instinct to just get as far away from the situation as possible.\n\nAnd seeing it? Oh, absolutely. If I look over and see one of the other guys—like my buddy Mike, he works the station right next to mine—if I see him pull his razor out of the Barbicide jar and I see that blade flipped open... man, I can't even look. I have to turn my whole body away. Even just seeing the blade exposed, just catching the light from the shop windows, it sends this shock straight through me. My stomach drops. \n\nI actually arrange my whole station so my own razors are completely hidden, like I was saying before, just so I don't accidentally glance at them while I'm reaching for my clippers or my shears. Because even just catching a glimpse of the handle sitting there, just knowing what it is, knowing the blade is tucked inside... my heart starts going. It's exhausting, honestly. You have no idea how exhausting it is to be constantly on guard, constantly scanning the room out of the corner of my eye to make sure no one is about to flip one open near me. I mean, it's a barbershop! They're everywhere! And I'm just standing there, trying to hold a normal, relaxed conversation about sports or the weather with my client, while inside I'm completely panicking just because Mike is shaving a guy three feet away from me. So, yeah, it doesn't even have to be me holding it. Just the thought of it, or the sight of it, is enough to set me off completely.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself getting anxious or preoccupied with worry about using the straight razor even before you come into work—like when you're at home the night before or thinking about your schedule?\n\nPatient: Actually, no. And I know that probably sounds a little contradictory, considering how much of a wreck I am when I'm actually there, but... no, I really don't. When I'm at home, it's like my brain just completely compartmentalizes the whole thing. \n\nLike, my evening routine is pretty set in stone. I leave the shop, I drive home, I make dinner—like I was talking about earlier with the cooking—and I just completely unplug. I used to be one of those guys who would obsessively check the booking app, you know, like Square Appointments or Booksy, just constantly refreshing it at 10 PM to see exactly who was on my schedule for the next morning, what services they booked, if there were any new walk-ins, all of that. But I stopped doing that a long time ago, even before all this razor stuff started, just for my own sanity. You really have to have a work-life balance in this industry or you burn out by the time you're thirty. \n\nSo because I don't check my schedule anymore, I don't really know who's coming in, which means I'm not sitting on my couch dreading, like, 'Oh man, Dave is coming in at 9 AM and he always wants a full hot towel face shave.' I just... I don't think about it. I sleep perfectly fine, honestly. Eight hours, out like a light. I wake up, make my coffee, get in my car... I usually listen to a podcast on the drive in, maybe some sports radio or an interview, and I'm totally relaxed. My heart rate is normal, I'm not sweating, I'm just a regular guy going to work. \n\nIt’s really not until... well, I guess it’s the moment I actually pull into the parking lot. Or, really, when I pull the handle on the front glass door to the shop and that smell hits you. You know that specific barbershop smell? The talcum powder, the sandalwood aftershave, the Barbicide? The literal second that smell hits my nose and I hear the clippers buzzing from the other stations, *that's* when the radar turns on. That's when my body remembers, 'Oh right, we have to be on high alert today.' But the night before? Or just hanging out at my apartment? No, not at all. It’s like the razor doesn’t even exist in my universe until I'm physically standing in the shop.\n\nDoctor: Do you also feel anxious or avoid things if you see a straight razor in a picture, on TV, or in a movie, or if someone talks about using one?\n\nPatient: You know, surprisingly... no. Not at all. It is actually kind of funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day. I was watching Peaky Blinders on TV—I don't know if you have seen it, it is set in England back in the twenties, really gritty, great cinematography, Cillian Murphy is just incredible in it—and the main characters literally have straight razor blades sewn right into the brims of their caps. They take their hats off and use them as weapons in these massive, chaotic street fights. And I was just sitting there on my couch, totally relaxed, not even blinking. My heart rate didn't go up, my hands were completely dry. I was just watching it like any normal person would watch a TV show. \n\nAnd it is the exact same thing with pictures or social media. Being a barber, my entire Instagram and TikTok feed is basically just hair tutorials and barbershop videos. It is just how the algorithm works, you know? You watch one fade tutorial and suddenly your whole explore page is guys doing these super detailed, macro-lens videos of hot towel shaves, where you see the straight razor gliding right over the skin in slow motion. And I can watch those all day long! I actually really appreciate them. My brain just goes into total analytical barber mode. It is only when the physical object is actually in the room with me, when it is real and tangible and the blade is actually exposed right in front of my face... that is when all the alarms start going off. But TV, movies, pictures, just talking about it... totally fine. It doesn't bother me in the slightest.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or avoid things if you see the case or hear the sound of a straight razor being opened, even when you're not at work?\n\nPatient: I mean, honestly... no, not really. Well, it's not really this slow, agonizing buildup where I'm just standing around all day wondering if it's going to happen. Like I was saying before, I really try to just live in the moment with whatever haircut I'm doing right then. If I'm doing a standard scissor cut or just a basic clipper fade, my mind is entirely on the fade. I'm talking to the guy about sports, or the weather, or whatever. 

But... it's the exact moment it becomes a reality. The literal second I hear a client ask for the razor shave—like, they'll just be sitting there, cape on, and casually go, "Hey, can you hit the neck with the straight blade today?" or "I think I want to do the full hot towel shave"—man, it is just instant. My chest completely tightens up. It feels like someone just yanked a strap tight around my ribs. And my hands get instantly, incredibly sweaty. Which, you know, as a barber, having sweaty palms is pretty much the worst thing ever when you're trying to grip metal shears and carefully manipulate someone's hair. I'll have to secretly wipe them on my jeans or grab a towel just to dry off.

And it doesn't even have to be my own client, honestly. If I'm just sweeping up hair around my chair, and out of the corner of my eye I see one of the other guys—like Tommy at the station next to me—if I just see him grab his razor and flip the blade open to start on his guy, it's the exact same reaction. It’s like my body just physically wants to back away before I even have a chance to think about it. It's this pure, raw instinct to just step backwards. I literally have to force my feet to stay planted on the anti-fatigue mat because my physical body is just trying to put distance between me and that open blade before my conscious brain even processes what's happening. 

So, yeah, it's not a lingering worry all morning. It's like a light switch. I'm totally fine, just doing my job, and then—bam. The request happens, or the blade swings open, and suddenly I can't breathe right, I'm sweating through my shirt, and my only instinct is to back up.

Honestly, no, not really. And I know that probably sounds a little weird, considering how intense my reaction is when it actually happens, but if it's just a possibility, or if it's scheduled for way later in the day, I don't really get worked up about it. 

Like, to give you an idea of how our shop works, we use this booking app—it's called Squire, a lot of modern barbershops use it now instead of just doing walk-ins or keeping a paper book, it just makes everything so much easier for the clients. So they'll go on the app, and they can select exactly what service they want, right? They'll pick "Standard Haircut" or "Skin Fade and Hot Towel Shave." 

So, I'll wake up in the morning, usually around 7:30 or so, and I'll make my coffee, and I'll just be sitting at my kitchen island scrolling through my schedule for the day on my phone. And I might see, clear as day, right there on the screen: "2:00 PM - Greg - Full Straight Razor Shave." And sitting there in my kitchen, looking at that? I feel absolutely nothing. No tight chest, no sweaty palms, no panic. I'll just take a sip of my coffee and think, "Okay, cool, busy afternoon." 

It's like my brain completely compartmentalizes it, you know? Because the razor isn't there. The threat isn't right in front of me. Even if I'm at the shop, and it's 1:00 PM, and I know Greg is coming in an hour, I'm just focused on the guy currently in my chair. I'm talking to him about his weekend or whatever, just doing a normal scissor cut. I'm not standing there shaking, dreading 2:00 PM. 

And it's the exact same thing with my coworkers. If Tommy is sweeping up next to me and he's like, "Man, my next guy always wants the straight blade on his head, it takes forever," I'll just be like, "Good luck, man, better you than me." I don't get that urge to back away or anything just from him talking about it or knowing he's going to do it in twenty minutes. 

It really, truly is just the immediate, physical presence of the thing. It's like my brain refuses to hit the panic button until the very last possible second. The moment Greg sits in my chair and I actually have to reach for the tool, or the moment Tommy physically flips his blade open at the station next to me... that's when the switch flips and all the physical stuff hits me. But just knowing it's on the schedule for later? Or knowing there's a chance someone might walk in and ask for it? No, I'm completely fine. I just go about my day like normal until the literal second it's happening right in front of me.

And I know that probably sounds a little contradictory, considering how much of a wreck I am when I'm actually there, but... no, I really don't. When I'm at home, it's like my brain just completely compartmentalizes the whole thing. \n\nLike, my evening routine is pretty set in stone. I leave the shop, I drive home, I make dinner—like I was talking about earlier with the cooking—and I just completely unplug. I used to be one of those guys who would obsessively check the booking app, you know, like Square Appointments or Booksy, just constantly refreshing it at 10 PM to see exactly who was on my schedule for the next morning, what services they booked, if there were any new walk-ins, all of that. But I stopped doing that a long time ago, even before all this razor stuff started, just for my own sanity. You really have to have a work-life balance in this industry or you burn out by the time you're thirty. \n\nSo because I don't check my schedule anymore, I don't really know who's coming in, which means I'm not sitting on my couch dreading, like, 'Oh man, Dave is coming in at 9 AM and he always wants a full hot towel face shave.' I just... I don't think about it. I sleep perfectly fine, honestly. Eight hours, out like a light. I wake up, make my coffee, get in my car... I usually listen to a podcast on the drive in, maybe some sports radio or an interview, and I'm totally relaxed. My heart rate is normal, I'm not sweating, I'm just a regular guy going to work. \n\nIt’s really not until... well, I guess it’s the moment I actually pull into the parking lot. Or, really, when I pull the handle on the front glass door to the shop and that smell hits you. You know that specific barbershop smell? The talcum powder, the sandalwood aftershave, the Barbicide? The literal second that smell hits my nose and I hear the clippers buzzing from the other stations, *that's* when the radar turns on. That's when my body remembers, 'Oh right, we have to be on high alert today.' But the night before? Or just hanging out at my apartment? No, not at all. It’s like the razor doesn’t even exist in my universe until I'm physically standing in the shop.\n\nDoctor: Do you also feel anxious or avoid things if you see a straight razor in a picture, on TV, or in a movie, or if someone talks about using one?\n\nPatient: You know, surprisingly... no. Not at all. It is actually kind of funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about this the other day. I was watching Peaky Blinders on TV—I don't know if you have seen it, it is set in England back in the twenties, really gritty, great cinematography, Cillian Murphy is just incredible in it—and the main characters literally have straight razor blades sewn right into the brims of their caps. They take their hats off and use them as weapons in these massive, chaotic street fights. And I was just sitting there on my couch, totally relaxed, not even blinking. My heart rate didn't go up, my hands were completely dry. I was just watching it like any normal person would watch a TV show. \n\nAnd it is the exact same thing with pictures or social media. Being a barber, my entire Instagram and TikTok feed is basically just hair tutorials and barbershop videos. It is just how the algorithm works, you know? You watch one fade tutorial and suddenly your whole explore page is guys doing these super detailed, macro-lens videos of hot towel shaves, where you see the straight razor gliding right over the skin in slow motion. And I can watch those all day long! I actually really appreciate them. I will look at the video and think, oh man, his blade angle is perfect, or I will wonder if he is using a Feather Artist Club razor or maybe a Parker handle. My brain just goes into total analytical barber mode. There is absolutely zero panic. \n\nEven if someone is just talking about it, like if I am out grabbing a coffee and a buddy mentions getting a really good straight razor shave at a shop downtown, I don't get that tight feeling in my chest at all. I can talk about the technique, the type of lather they used, the history of the tools, all of it, and I am completely fine. \n\nSo it is definitely not the concept of the razor, if that makes sense. It is like my brain is smart enough to know that a picture on a screen or a video on my phone cannot physically reach out and hurt anybody. It is trapped behind the glass, so it is safe. It is only when the physical object is actually in the room with me, when it is real and tangible and the blade is actually exposed right in front of my face... that is when all the alarms start going off. But TV, movies, pictures, just talking about it... totally fine. It doesn't bother me in the slightest.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel anxious or avoid things if you see the case or hear the sound of a straight razor being opened, even when you're not at work?\n\nPatient: I mean, honestly... no, not really. I don't really encounter cases or hear that sound outside of the shop, you know? It's just not something you run into at the grocery store or whatever. But even if I did, like, say I was at an antique store or something—which my girlfriend loves going to on weekends, she’s really into mid-century modern furniture and vintage glassware and all that, so we spend a lot of time just wandering around these massive antique malls—if I saw an old straight razor case in a display cabinet, I don't think it would really bother me. Because, again, it's just a case. It's an object. \n\nIt's the same with the sound. The sound of a razor flipping open... it's a very specific click, you know? Outside of work? It's like a totally different world. I'm just a normal guy, doing normal guy things, and razors aren't even on my radar.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever start feeling anxious as soon as you know that you might have to use a straight razor during the day, even if it's not yet in your hand or someone hasn't asked for it?\n\nPatient: Well, it's not really this slow, agonizing buildup where I'm just standing around all day wondering if it's going to happen. I'll have to secretly wipe them on my jeans or grab a towel just to dry off.\n\nAnd it doesn't even have to be my own client, honestly. It’s like my body just physically wants to back away before I even have a chance to think about it. It's this pure, raw instinct to just step backwards. I literally have to force my feet to stay planted on the anti-fatigue mat because my physical body is just trying to put distance between me and that open blade before my conscious brain even processes what's happening. \n\nSo, yeah, it's not a lingering worry all morning. It's like a light switch. I'm totally fine, just doing my job, and then—bam. The request happens, or the blade swings open, and suddenly I can't breathe right, I'm sweating through my shirt, and my only instinct is to back up.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever start to feel anxious or physically uncomfortable in situations where you know there's a chance you might encounter a straight razor, even if you haven't seen one yet—like if you're told someone might request a hot shave later in the day, or if a coworker mentions they're going to use their razor soon?\n\nPatient: Honestly, no, not really. And I know that probably sounds a little weird, considering how intense my reaction is when it actually happens, but if it's just a possibility, or if it's scheduled for way later in the day, I don't really get worked up about it. \n\nLike, to give you an idea of how our shop works, we use this booking app—it's called Squire, a lot of modern barbershops use it now instead of just doing walk-ins or keeping a paper book, it just makes everything so much easier for the clients. I just go about my day like normal until the literal second it's happening right in front of me.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever start feeling anxious in the hours before you know you'll have to use the straight razor—like, say, an hour or two beforehand—or does the anxiety only hit you in the exact moment it's happening?\n\nPatient: Yeah, like I was kind of just saying a minute ago, it really doesn't build up over a couple of hours. I know we’re really drilling down into the exact timeline here, and I feel like I’m just giving you the same answer over and over, but it really is the truth—even at one or two minutes out, I am completely fine.

I’ve already put the paper neck strip on him, I’ve draped the cutting cape over him and clipped it tight. All of that takes maybe sixty to ninety seconds before the actual shave begins. And during all of that? I am totally calm. My heart rate is completely normal. No, no, not at all. The prep tools don't bother me one bit. I mean, I know we've been talking a lot about the buildup and the timing, but honestly, looking at the lather bowl or the hot towel cabinet, or even holding the bottle of pre-shave oil... it just doesn't trigger anything in me. I can clean out the lather machine at the end of the day, I can restock all the oils, I can fold a hundred towels and load up the UV sterilizer, and I'm totally at peace. They're just inanimate objects to me. 

Because, see, the thing is... I know it's all just equipment. And honestly, logically, I know the straight razor is just a tool I trained with, too. I mean, I went to barber school, I graduated, I put in hundreds of hours on the floor to get my license. I know how to do this. I can use clippers all day long, right? I can do a tight skin fade, I can edge up a beard with my trimmers, I can use my sharpest shears right next to a guy's ear or his neck, and I don't even think twice about it. I'm totally confident with all of it. 

But... and this is the part that just drives me crazy because it makes absolutely zero logical sense... when that straight razor is sitting open at my station, it feels like I’m about to hurt somebody or cut myself badly. 

It's like all my training and all those hours of practice just fly right out the window the second the blade is exposed. I look at that sharp edge, and my brain just immediately jumps to the worst-case scenario.
